newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Thai central bank moves to squeeze out speculators.
newsitem.headline: Thai central bank moves to squeeze out speculators.

text.p: The Bank of Thailand's move to engineer a liquidity squeeze on Thursday spurred a strong rebound in the baht as speculators who had aggressively shorted the currency were forced to cover their positions, dealers said.

They said the central bank had instructed local banks not to quote tom/next to offshore parties, effectively removing an avenue for overseas players to borrow baht to cover short positions established when the currency was heavily sold.
He added that players were forced to sell dollars against baht on the spot market to cover their short positions.
Dealers said the tom/next reached a high of 200 satangs.
"Everybody's just trying to fight for survival, they're just scrambling for funds," another dealer said.
He said there was no need for the central bank to intervene in currency markets to support the baht as it did on Wednesday.

"It was an extremely smart and logical move for the central bank and the result shows that it was effective. It's a less expensive way of achieving the same purpose (as intervention)," said Andy Tan, regional economist at MMS Standard & Poor's.
He said the central bank was likely to keep liquidity on a tight leash until the market stabilised. The possibility of another speculative attack on the baht could not be ruled out, he added.
"In this first round, the Thai central bank has come out on top, but it's too early to tell if this is the end," Tan said.
The U.S. bank dealer said Thursday's move had flushed out the short-term speculators but left the longer term hedge funds relatively unscathed.

"All the big speculators who were short the baht and long dollars had covered on a much longer term basis, like six months or one year. So the short-term liquidity didn't matter much to them," he said.
"It's only the smaller speculators who tried to jump on the bandwagon and follow the trend who got killed," he said.
He said the tom/next rate had come off but could go back up towards 100 satangs on Friday.

"Today just represents the kind of band-aid solutions Thailand has been applying over the past year rather than coming up with a consistent policy to deal with a combination of cylical and structural changes in the economy," said Song Seng Wun, regional economist at ABN-AMRO Hoare Govett.

Although the BOT was forced to defend the baht this week to prevent a stock market collapse, Song said Thai authorities needed to look at longer term fiscal measures to prevent further attacks on the baht.
